name: Fat Flush Plan

lead: The Fat Flush Plan is a diet-and-exercise program created by American nutritionist and author Ann Louise Gittleman and published as a book in the early 2000s. It is framed as a 'detox' plan, and people use it with the aim of losing body fat and water weight for a leaner, less bloated appearance.

It became a New York Times best seller and spawned follow-up books, including The Gut Flush Plan (2008) and Fat Flush for Life (2010). Reviewers and obesity specialists have criticized its detox premise, and no published trial has tested the plan itself.

paras: Followers adopt the plan as a structured eating program accompanied by exercise, typically for a defined period, often after reading one of Gittleman's books. Details of the phases are set out in the books themselves.

Nutrition experts quoted in coverage, including Judith Stern of the American Obesity Society, have called the plan's detox rationale pseudoscience. As with other restrictive diets, people with medical conditions, those who are pregnant, and those with a history of disordered eating are generally advised by clinicians to seek individual guidance first.

angle.text: Followers use the plan as a structured program for weight and bloat reduction, with the visible aim of a leaner midsection and face. As with other calorie-structured diets, weight change largely tracks how much a person's intake falls.

lead: The Fat Flush Plan is a diet and exercise program devised by Ann Louise Gittleman, an American author and self-described nutritionist. It was released in 2001 and published by McGraw-Hill (listed as 2002), and it reached number 14 on the New York Times 'Hardcover Advice' list [1]. The plan is presented as a detox that encourages the body to 'flush' fat and toxins.

People who follow it are generally pursuing a leaner look: less body fat, less water retention and a flatter midsection. In looksmaxxing circles it is grouped with fringe or 'liver-cleanse' style diets that promise visible changes in body composition through a short structured program.

Gittleman extended the concept in later books, including The Gut Flush Plan (2008) and Fat Flush for Life (2010) [1]. The plan was also discussed in a 2004 Time article on low-carb diets [1]. Critics, including Judith Stern of the American Obesity Society, have described the approach as pseudoscience, and reviewers say the books present research in a simplified, one-sided way [1]. No clinical trial of the Fat Flush Plan itself is known.

New York Times best seller; criticized by nutrition experts

paras: The plan is a 'detox' diet and exercise program, built around the idea that cleansing the body supports fat loss [1]. Specific steps and phases are laid out in Gittleman's books.

Gittleman published the original book in 2001 (listed with a 2002 McGraw-Hill release). It reached the New York Times best-seller list and was covered in a 2004 Time article on low-carb diets, and she later published The Gut Flush Plan (2008) and Fat Flush for Life (2010) [1].

Wikipedia reports that Gittleman's ideas are regarded as pseudoscience and that critics say her books present research simplistically. Judith Stern of the American Obesity Society called the plan 'pseudoscience' and 'a fantasy', and a 2009 New York Times piece on detox diets carried the headline 'Flush Those Toxins! Eh, Not So Fast' [1]. Proponents, for their part, describe the plan as a structured way to lose weight and feel less bloated.
